title: USCIS Revokes H-1B Petitions After IT Firm Classified Jobs Below Required Wage Levels
excerpt: The agency's Vermont office found a major IT consulting company placed skilled technology positions at wage levels that did not match the duties and requirements of the roles, undercutting protections for American workers.
body:
• USCIS denied and revoked multiple H-1B petitions filed by an unnamed major IT consulting company over wage-level misclassification.
  • The agency's Vermont office found the company classified skilled technology jobs at wage levels below what the positions' duties and requirements supported.
  • USCIS said the practice undercuts required wages and creates unfair competition for American workers.
  • The agency did not name the company, disclose how many petitions were affected, or specify which technology positions were involved.

US Citizenship and Immigration Services has denied and revoked multiple H-1B visa petitions after determining that a major IT consulting company systematically classified skilled technology positions at wage levels that did not match the actual duties and requirements of the jobs.

The agency disclosed the enforcement action in a post on X, stating that its Vermont office identified the wage-level discrepancies during a routine review of H-1B cases.

"USCIS in Vermont identified H-1B petitions from a major IT consulting company that classified skilled technology jobs at wage levels below what the positions' duties and requirements supported. This practice undercuts required wages and creates unfair competition for U.S. workers."

— USCIS

How Wage-Level Misclassification Works

Under the H-1B program, employers sponsoring foreign workers must meet applicable wage requirements for the positions they seek to fill. The Department of Labor establishes four wage levels for each occupation and geographic area, ranging from entry-level (Level 1) to fully competent (Level 4).

https://x.com/USCIS/status/2095968109127426378

When a company assigns a skilled position to a lower wage level than the role's duties warrant, it reduces the prevailing wage threshold the employer must meet. This can result in foreign workers being paid less than what the market requires for that level of work, while simultaneously making it harder for American workers to compete for similar positions.

USCIS did not accuse the company of criminal fraud in its public statement. The action instead reflects the agency's focus on whether H-1B positions are being classified and compensated in a manner consistent with their actual responsibilities.

Broader Enforcement Context

The revocations come during a period of intensified scrutiny of H-1B applications from IT consulting companies under the Trump administration. IT consulting and staffing firms have historically faced higher denial rates than major technology companies, with some consultancies seeing denial rates as high as 40 percent compared to approximately 1 percent for companies like Microsoft, Google, and Amazon.

The action also follows a series of federal criminal cases involving alleged H-1B fraud in the IT staffing sector. In April 2025, the owner of a San Jose-based technology staffing firm was sentenced to 14 months in prison after pleading guilty to submitting fraudulent H-1B applications claiming workers had jobs at designated client companies when those positions did not exist.

More recently, in April 2026, two East Bay men pleaded guilty to conspiring to commit H-1B visa fraud after prosecutors said they submitted petitions falsely representing that foreign workers would be employed on projects for the University of California.

What Remains Unknown

USCIS has not disclosed the identity of the IT consulting company at the center of the Vermont investigation. The agency also withheld the number of petitions affected and the specific technology positions that were reviewed.

The lack of detail has drawn attention on social media, where users have speculated about whether the unnamed firm is one of the major Indian IT consulting companies that dominate H-1B filings. USCIS has not addressed those inquiries.

For H-1B employers, particularly those in the technology consulting sector, the action signals that USCIS may increasingly scrutinize whether the wage level assigned to a position is consistent with the job's actual duties and requirements, rather than accepting classifications at face value.

"We denied and revoked multiple petitions, protecting American workers and preserving the integrity of employment-based immigration programs."

— USCIS

As the agency continues its review of employment-based immigration cases, the Vermont investigation adds another layer of enforcement pressure on companies that rely heavily on the H-1B program.
